elements.id-string-12: One of the central tasks in many-body physics is the determination of phase diagrams, which can be cast as a classification problem.
elements.id-string-13: Typically, classification problems are tackled using discriminative classifiers that explicitly model the conditional probability of labels given a sample.
elements.id-string-14: Here we show that phase-classification problems are naturally suitable to be solved using generative classifiers that are based on probabilistic models of the measurement statistics underlying the physical system.
elements.id-string-15: Such a generative approach benefits from modeling concepts native to the realm of statistical and quantum physics, as well as recent advances in machine learning.
elements.id-string-16: This yields a powerful framework for mapping out phase diagrams of classical and quantum systems in an automated fashion that is capable of leveraging prior system knowledge.
elements.id-string-17: \emph{Introduction}.---A classification task can be approached in two fundamentally distinct ways~\cite{ng:2001}.
elements.id-string-18: Typically, a classifier is constructed by modeling the conditional probability $P(y|\bm{x})$ of label $y$ given a sample $\bm{x}$ directly [see Fig.~\ref{fig:1}(a)].
elements.id-string-19: Models of this type are called discriminative and the corresponding classifier predicts the label $y$ that maximizes $P(y|\bm{x})$.
elements.id-string-20: Discriminative classifiers have had tremendous success in fields such as image classification in large part due to the power of neural networks, particularly convolutional neural networks~\cite{krizhevsky:2012}.
elements.id-string-21: The alternative is to model the conditional probability of a sample given a label $P(\bm{x}|y)$ [see Fig.~\ref{fig:1}(b)].
elements.id-string-22: Such models are called generative models as they describe how to generate samples $\bm{x}$ conditioned on the class label $y$~\cite{gen_vs_disc}.
elements.id-string-25: one can use a generative model to construct a so-called generative classifier.
elements.id-string-26: Generative models are apt for describing high-dimensional probability distributions.
elements.id-string-27: As such, they have played a pivotal role in recent advances in machine learning, enabling applications such as the generation of images, translation of text, or composition of music~\cite{vaswani:2017}.
elements.id-string-28: Moreover, the generative modeling approach is naturally suited to address problems in many-body physics, which often deals with the fundamental challenge of describing probability distributions over large state spaces.
elements.id-string-29: In statistical physics, Boltzmann distributions have been described by generative models ranging from mean-field ansatzes to autoregressive networks~\cite{wu:2019}.
elements.id-string-30: Similarly, various approaches have been developed to express quantum states, including mean-field ansatzes and tensor networks~\cite{schollwock:2011}, as well as machine-learning inspired generative models, such as restricted Boltzmann machines~\cite{carleo:2017}, or recurrent neural networks~\cite{hibat:2020}, and transformers~\cite{cha:2021}.
elements.id-string-31: \indent One of the most important tasks in many-body physics is the characterization of phase diagrams~\cite{goldenfeld:2018,sachdev:2011}.
elements.id-string-32: Traditionally, this is done by identifying a small set of physical quantities, like response functions or order parameters, guided by human intuition.
elements.id-string-33: An exciting recent development has been the usage of machine learning methods to automate this task, replacing the physicist in the process~\cite{dawid:2022}.
elements.id-string-34: To this end, the problem of mapping out a phase diagram is, e.g., cast as a classification task~\cite{carrasquilla:2017,van:2017,schaefer:2019}.
elements.id-string-35: By solving these classification tasks using discriminative classifiers, the phase diagrams of a large variety of physical systems have successfully been revealed in both simulation~\cite{carrasquilla:2017,van:2017,schaefer:2019,liu:2018,beach:2018,suchsland:2018,lee:2019,greplova:2020,arnold:2021,gavreev:2022,zvyagintseva:2022,schlomer:2023} and experiment~\cite{rem:2019,bohrdt:2021,miles:2023}.

elements.id-string-99: \indent The main idea of this Letter is to approach the problem of mapping out a phase diagram in a generative manner.
elements.id-string-100: Given a model of the probability distributions underlying the measurement statistics at various discrete points in parameter space $\{ \tilde{P}(\bm{x}|\bm{\gamma}) \}_{\bm{\gamma} \in \Gamma}$ from which one can efficiently sample, an estimate of an indicator [Eqs.~\eqref{eq:ISL}, \eqref{eq:ILBC}, and~\eqref{eq:IPBM}] can be computed by substituting $P(\bm{x}|\bm{\gamma})$ with $\tilde{P}(\bm{x}|\bm{\gamma})$ and replacing the expectation value with a sample mean $\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x} \sim P(\bm{x}|\bm{\gamma})} \rightarrow \frac{1}{|\tilde{\mathcal{D}}_{\bm{\gamma}}|}\sum_{\bm{x} \in \tilde{\mathcal{D}}_{\bm{\gamma}}}$, where $\tilde{\mathcal{D}}_{\bm{\gamma}}$ denotes the set of samples drawn from the model $\tilde{P}(\bm{x}|\bm{\gamma})$.

elements.id-string-116: \indent \emph{Classical equilibrium systems}.---For a classical system at equilibrium with a large thermal reservoir, the probability to find the system in state $\bm{x} \in \mathcal{X}$ is given by $P(\bm{x}| \bm{\gamma}) = e^{-\mathcal{H}(\bm{x},\bm{\gamma})}/Z(\bm{\gamma})$,
elements.id-string-118: Here, we consider dimensionless Hamiltonians of the form $\mathcal{H} = H/k_{\rm B}T = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \gamma_{i} X_{i}(\bm{x})$.
elements.id-string-119: The large state space $\mathcal{X}$ renders modeling such distributions a hard task.
elements.id-string-120: However, such Boltzmann distributions belong to the exponential family and $\bm{X} = \left( X_{1}(\bm{x}), \dots, X_{d}(\bm{x}) \right)$ is a minimal sufficient statistic for $\bm{\gamma}$, i.e., the map $\bm{x} \rightarrow \bm{X}$ corresponds to an optimal lossless compression with respect to $\bm{\gamma}$.
elements.id-string-121: Thus, to map out phase diagrams by computing an indicator it suffices to model $\{ P(\bm{X}|\bm{\gamma})\}_{\bm{\gamma} \in \Gamma}$ (proof in~\cite{suppl}).

elements.id-string-153: \emph{Conclusions}.---In this Letter, we have introduced generative classifiers as alternatives to discriminative classifiers to solve the classification tasks required for mapping out phase diagrams in an autonomous fashion.
elements.id-string-154: The generative approach naturally allows for the incorporation of system knowledge, such as the Hamiltonian or the functional form of the relevant family of probability distributions.
elements.id-string-155: This makes it favorable for numerical investigations where such information is readily available.
elements.id-string-156: We have explicitly demonstrated this advantage for classical systems in equilibrium as well as quantum ground states.
elements.id-string-157: Extensions to classical nonequilibrium systems, as well as other quantum states, are possible by adapting the generative model.
elements.id-string-158: If system knowledge is scarce, e.g., when characterizing quantum states prepared in an experiment~\cite{carrasquilla:2019,gomez:2022}, generative models can also be constructed in a data-driven manner.
elements.id-string-159: This makes generative classifiers extremely versatile and applicable in various contexts.
elements.id-string-160: Since generative models play a fundamental role in many-body physics, it is expected that many more classification tasks in this domain can benefit from a generative approach.

elements.id-string-175: In traditional discriminative machine learning (ML) tasks, class imbalance occurs when the number of samples representing each class within the data set differs.
elements.id-string-176: In phase-classification tasks, this can, for example, occur when one does not have access to an equal amount of data at each point in parameter space.
elements.id-string-177: Moreover, in scheme 1 (with indicator $I_{1}$) and 2 (with indicator $I_{2}$) discussed in the main text, an imbalance can also occur when sampling an \emph{equal} amount of data at each point in parameter space.
elements.id-string-178: In both cases, the imbalance arises because the sets $\{ \Gamma_{y}\}_{y \in \mathcal{Y}}$ are not of equal size.
elements.id-string-179: In scheme 1, this can be circumvented by choosing an equal number of points in parameter space to represent each phase.
elements.id-string-180: In scheme 2, data sets of unequal size occur as the bipartitions artificially divide the uniformly sampled one-dimensional parameter space.
elements.id-string-181: In previous works~\cite{van:2017,liu:2018,beach:2018,suchsland:2018,lee:2019,greplova:2020,bohrdt:2021,richter:2022,gavreev:2022,zvyagintseva:2022,schlomer:2023}, this class imbalance was not accounted for.
elements.id-string-182: As a result, the corresponding indicator $I_{2}$ will exhibit trivial local maxima ($I_{2}=1$) at the edges of the sampled region of the parameter space where the entire data is labeled 1 or 2, respectively.
elements.id-string-183: If no phase transition is present, the indicator will thus exhibit a characteristic V-shape.
elements.id-string-184: In the presence of a phase transition, a W-shape is expected, where the location of the intermediate maximum corresponds to the predicted critical point.

elements.id-string-341: One of the central tasks in many-body physics is the determination of phase diagrams.
elements.id-string-342: However, mapping out a phase diagram generally requires a great deal of human intuition and understanding.
elements.id-string-343: To automate this process, one can frame it as a classification task.
elements.id-string-344: Typically, classification problems are tackled using discriminative classifiers that explicitly model the probability of the labels for a given sample.
elements.id-string-345: Here we show that phase-classification problems are naturally suitable to be solved using generative classifiers based on probabilistic models of the measurement statistics underlying the physical system.
elements.id-string-346: This leads to a powerful framework for the autonomous determination of phase diagrams with little to no human supervision that we showcase in applications to classical equilibrium systems and quantum ground states.
elements.id-string-347: Models of this type are called discriminative and the corresponding classifier predicts the label $y$ with maximal $P(y|\bm{x})$.
elements.id-string-348: Due to the power of neural networks (NNs), particularly convolutional NNs~\cite{krizhevsky:2012}, discriminative classifiers have had tremendous success in fields such as image classification.
elements.id-string-349: \indent Generative models have played a pivotal role in recent advances in machine learning, enabling applications such as the generation of images, composition of music, or translation of text~\cite{vaswani:2017}.
elements.id-string-350: Moreover, generative models have been used extensively to describe many-body systems.
elements.id-string-351: In statistical physics, Boltzmann distributions have been represented by generative models ranging from mean-field ansatzes to autoregressive networks~\cite{wu:2019}.
elements.id-string-352: Similarly, various approaches have been developed to express quantum states, including mean-field ansatzes and tensor networks~\cite{schollwock:2011}, as well as novel machine-learning-inspired generative models, such as restricted Boltzmann machines~\cite{carleo:2017}, or recurrent NNs~\cite{hibat:2020}, and transformers~\cite{cha:2021}.
elements.id-string-353: Traditionally, this is done by identifying a small set of low-dimensional physical quantities like response functions or order parameters.
elements.id-string-354: The large number of degrees of freedom makes finding such quantities difficult, and success generally requires a great deal of human intuition and understanding.
elements.id-string-355: In particular, it can be challenging to identify an order parameter without knowing the symmetry-breaking pattern or in the absence of local order.
elements.id-string-356: An exciting recent development has been the automation of this scientific process through machine learning methods~\cite{carleo:2019,terayama:2019,guan:2020,dawid:2022} by exploiting their ability to distill key information from large amounts of high-dimensional data.
elements.id-string-357: To this end, the problem of mapping out a phase diagram can be cast as a classification task~\cite{carrasquilla:2017,van:2017,wetzel2:2017,schaefer:2019}.
elements.id-string-358: By solving such classification tasks in a data-driven manner using discriminative classifiers, the phase diagrams of a large variety of physical systems have successfully been revealed in both simulation~\cite{carrasquilla:2017,van:2017,wetzel2:2017,schaefer:2019,liu:2018,beach:2018,suchsland:2018,lee:2019,kharkov:2020,guo:2020,greplova:2020,arnold:2021,gavreev:2022,zvyagintseva:2022,tibaldi:2023,guo:2023,schlomer:2023} and experiment~\cite{rem:2019,bohrdt:2021,miles:2023}.
elements.id-string-359: Because generic data, such as spin configurations or energy spectra, can be used as input, this constitutes a promising route toward the discovery of novel phases of matter and phase transitions with little to no human supervision.
